title: Sharing Among the Human Capitalists: An Economic Inquiry into the Corporate Law Firm and How Partners Split Profits
pub: Stanford Law Review, vol. 37, no. 2, pp. 313-392 (Jan. 1985) (Symposium on the Law Firm as a Social Institution)
author: Ronald J. Gilson · Robert H. Mnookin

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: The source supports the narrower claim that general counsel redistribute purchasing power and may increase competition through more sophisticated procurement. It does not address the cluster’s principal concern that business integration can weaken professional resistance to harmful client demands, nor its case for reciprocal duties or contextual regulation.
qs: While they can play a number of important roles for the corporation, the most important role in terms of making the market for legal serv- ices more competitive is that of "purchasing agent." General counsel are the executives who decide what legal services are purchased and from whom.

It certainly appears that general counsel are becoming increasingly sophisticated about these decisions, and more knowledgeable                  0                              about how to make the marketplace more effective.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source accepts that large-firm durability cannot be explained by size alone and materially develops the proposition by identifying profit sharing and human-capital risk diversification as mechanisms supporting institutional stability. It also explains why sophisticated in-house buyers may weaken brand and firm-specific advantages without eliminating the benefits of diversified firms.
qs: In this article, we shed new light on the internal organization of law firms and the relationship of organizational structure to changes in the market for legal services by showing how a law firm can provide the opportunity for individual lawyers to diver- sify the risks inherent in human capital.
While the increased sophistication of pur- chasers should decrease reliance on the brand name of the large "department store" firms, the "cost savings" of diversification re- main.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The article does not address AI or faster matter completion directly, but materially extends the cluster’s economic account by identifying corporate insourcing, multisourcing and buyer switching power as mechanisms that can eliminate profits from routine associate work and weaken firm-specific capital. It therefore supports the view that profit outcomes depend on buyer behaviour and firm structure rather than hours alone.
qs: Such work will therefore no longer remain a source of extra profits in the future, and to that extent firm-specific capital will diminish.

The ability to rely on several firms can, among other things, enable companies to signal their current law firms that they are ready, willing, and able to shift their work to other firms should they be faced with unfavorable shifts in quality or price.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: The source supplies a foundational economic mechanism for the cluster’s systemic account: profit sharing diversifies human-capital risk but remains vulnerable to partner opportunism, mobility and delayed-reward risk. It materially extends the tournament framing by showing that competition and instability persist within partnership, especially for junior partners whose rewards depend on the firm’s continued success.
qs: We conclude that, contrary to the new conventional wisdom, because sharing facilitates diversification, the sharing model is superior, provided that shirking, grabbing, and leaving can be constrained.
An en- tering lawyer faces the risk that the firm may suffer a decline or even break up before he or she reaches the top.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source materially extends the cluster’s proposition by explaining partnership stability through firm-specific capital and profit sharing rather than capital availability alone. It also anticipates buyer-side insourcing of routine work as a threat to associate-generated surplus, showing that pressures on partnership organization predate generative AI and vary with firms’ underlying capital and client relationships.
qs: In a sense, then, our analysis suggests a paradox: "Sharing" enhances the success of successful firms with substantial firm-specific capital while con-  tributing to the instability of less successful firms without much firm-specific capital.
We predict that more and more corporations will continue to bring routine or repetitive legal work in-house.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI capability directly, but it materially extends the cluster’s work-redesign thesis with an economic mechanism: sophisticated in-house counsel can internalise routine work, selectively source specialist work and thereby weaken law firms’ firm-specific capital and traditional profit-sharing arrangements. Its qualifications about residual firm advantages also accord with restructuring rather than wholesale displacement.
qs: We predict that more and more corporations will continue to bring routine or repetitive legal work in-house.
As a result, we predict that the increased sophistication of general counsel in purchasing legal services will reduce the value of firm-specific capital.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central proposition by locating market power in general counsel’s purchasing and coordination role. It predicts more insourcing and erosion of incumbent firms’ information-based advantages and routine-work profits, but not wholesale displacement: sophisticated buyers can continue using multiple outside firms.
qs: While they can play a number of important roles for the corporation, the most important role in terms of making the market for legal serv- ices more competitive is that of "purchasing agent." General counsel are the executives who decide what legal services are purchased and from whom.
As a result, general coun- sel can reduce their companies' dependence on one firm, and thus facilitate the concurrent use of a number of law firms.

st.t: Market reform: Information and incentives shape access
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition that legal-market outcomes depend on information and incentives, not merely provider numbers or credentials. It explains how switching costs and uncertainty impede firm selection, distinguishes technical quality from necessary client value, and shows how a general counsel’s personal risk aversion can favour a defensible brand over the best fit.
qs: change firms, it would have to incur the cost of securing informa- tion about the quality of a rival law firm's services, a problem that is exacerbated the greater the client's risk aversion .

In this sense, a general counsel may have two goals in selecting a law firm: choos- ing a good firm, and choosing a firm, whether or not actually the best for the matter, whose selection will seem sensible to his superiors even if the legal effort proves unsuccessful.

kp.k: Historical theory explains profit sharing, not AI adoption
kp.d: This January 1985 article develops a theoretical explanation of corporate law firms using portfolio theory and agency theory. It addresses diversification, compensation, institutional stability and changing corporate purchasing practices, rather than AI. The authors present hypotheses requiring empirical investigation, not a systematically validated account of profit allocation.
qs: Our framework builds on the foundation of recent developments in two areas of economic the- ory: portfolio theory and the economic theory of agency.
To our knowledge, there has been no systematic empirical study of how large law firms- either currently or historically-have allocated partnership prof- its.

kp.k: Growth and instability challenge conventional explanations
kp.d: The authors juxtapose large-firm expansion with contemporary reports of collapses, departures and compensation disputes. Their historical evidence includes Shearman & Sterling having 134 attorneys as the largest American firm in 1963, versus 109 firms exceeding that size in 1983. They argue that scale, specialization, scope and minimum project size alone inadequately explain very large firms; boutiques demonstrate that specialization does not require large size.
qs: In 1983, 109 American firms had more than 134 attorneys.
the existence of smaller "boutique" law firms plainly shows that specialization is possible regardless of firm size.

kp.k: Sharing diversifies otherwise concentrated human capital
kp.d: The central mechanism is that lawyers invest heavily in earning capacity that cannot readily be sold or diversified. Insurance covers some risks, such as death and disability, but adverse selection and moral hazard obstruct insurance against disappointing careers and certain personal disruptions. Pooling earnings offers an institutional means of reducing these risks, although diversification within legal practice is not complete diversification across industries.
qs: A law- yer's earnings thus represent the return on his investment in human capital.
These risks share the twin problems of adverse selection and moral hazard that combine to make tradi- tional insurance infeasible.
complete diversification would require diversifying into other industries as well.

kp.k: Specialization strengthens the rationale for income pooling
kp.d: Specialization can increase expected earnings while concentrating exposure to changing demand. The authors illustrate this with hypothetical securities and bankruptcy practices, each yielding expected additional earnings of $100,000; equal investment in their perfectly offsetting returns eliminates variation in the example. They expressly caution that actual demand for these specialties may move together or respond at different times. The argument supports full-service firms as mechanisms for sharing specialization risks, not an empirical estimate of diversification benefits.
qs: Both investments, how- ever, present substantial risk; there is a 1/3 probability that the lawyer would earn no return at all on either investment.
We recognize that the relationship between a venture capital practice and a bankruptcy practice described in the text, while rhetorically helpful, may in reality be inaccurate.

kp.k: Shirking, grabbing and leaving threaten sharing bargains
kp.d: The authors distinguish insufficient effort, demands for larger shares backed by departure threats, and actual departures with clients. Sharing is attractive before individual outcomes are known, but successful partners may subsequently prefer to retain their earnings. Because the article treats employment specific performance and lawyer noncompetition covenants as unavailable in its contemporary legal setting, organizational incentives must make sharing self-enforcing.
qs: shirking, a partner's failure to do his "fair share" of the work;
The two re- sponses, of course, are closely related; it is the threat of leaving that allows grabbing to be successful.
Specific enforcement of employment obligations is not available in the real world and covenants not to compete among lawyers are not enforceable.

kp.k: Lockstep exchanges individual returns for a diversified portfolio
kp.d: In the authors' pure lockstep model, partners within an admission cohort receive identical shares and progress along predetermined steps toward full shares. This pools risks across individuals, specialties and generations. Although alternative compensation trajectories can theoretically have equivalent present values, delayed rewards expose entrants to firm decline or dissolution and can strengthen incentives for productive young partners to leave; excessively front-loaded rewards create different incentive problems.
qs: all partners in a single class earn the same income;
a partner's class depends only upon the year he was ad- mitted to the partnership and cannot be changed;
A high ratio and a long road to parity mean that the partnership payoff is heavily weighted towards a lawyer's later years.

kp.k: Productivity formulas introduce measurement errors and distorted incentives
kp.d: The authors challenge consultants' preference for productivity-based compensation. Hours, billing rates and client-origination credits imperfectly measure actual contribution and can encourage partners to optimize measured activities instead of firm profitability. Hours-based systems may underreward management and business development, discourage efficient referrals and penalize faster lawyers. Origination formulas can encourage client hoarding and disputes when client loyalty shifts to the lawyer doing the work.
qs: Partners are given an incen- tive to maximize their own income by maximizing the factors measured by the formula, rather than by actually maximizing their productivity.
Our simple formula meas- ures only effort, not results.
A lawyer gets no reward for attracting more clients than he or she can service alone.

kp.k: Firm-specific capital makes sharing economically sustainable
kp.d: Firm-specific capital is the excess value of the ongoing institution over what its lawyers could earn in their next-best outside uses. Unlike readily replicated scale economies, it cannot easily accompany a departing partner. Losing access to its returns can deter departures and weaken demands for larger shares. The authors use reported Cravath earnings in 1983—$855,000 for full-share partners and $285,000 for the youngest partners—as an illustrative, conditional explanation of stable lockstep, not causal proof.
qs: Without a realistic threat of leaving for more money, an attempt to grab is likely to be ineffective.
the full-share partners in Cravath each earned $855,000 in 1983, while the youngest partners enjoyed annual earnings of $285,000-a three-to-one ratio.
if there is no individual partner who upon leaving the firm, can take IBM with him, then the client relationship with IBM is an asset of the firm.

kp.k: Client relationships support staffing efficiency and switching advantages
kp.d: Predictable routine work allows efficient staffing and profits from employing associates, while a diversified client portfolio can make aggregate demand predictable even when individual clients' needs fluctuate. Investments in client knowledge, trust and working procedures create switching costs for both parties. These relationships become firm-specific assets only insofar as an individual or departing team cannot take or recreate them.
qs: Excess capacity-more lawyers than work-reduces returns.
Once this investment has been made, the incumbent firm has a signifi- cant cost advantage over potential competitors.
For that client, the particular group of lawyers is the firm.

kp.k: Reputation reduces uncertainty about legal service quality
kp.d: Clients can struggle to judge quality before purchase and even after delivery, because outcomes also reflect factors beyond counsel's control. The authors distinguish indirect quality signals from direct investigation. Sophisticated buyers can assess publications, seminars and particular lawyers more effectively, whereas general firm reputation can reduce search costs across specialties. Building individual reputations can also increase lawyers' outside opportunities and undermine retention.
qs: The market for legal services is characterized by significant problems of quality uncertainty.
it is helpful to distinguish between "searching" and "signaling."
Writing and lecturing by individual lawyers inevita- bly builds individual reputations and capital as well as firm- specific capital.

kp.k: Compensation affects reputation, independence and client ownership
kp.d: The authors argue that sharing better aligns partners with institutional client relationships and firm reputation, while productivity compensation encourages investment in portable clients and individual standing. They also describe law firms as reputational intermediaries that lend credibility to clients. Dependence on a client can weaken that credibility; where individual compensation depends heavily on a particular client, the relevant independence problem can arise at partner rather than firm level.
qs: Productivity formulas institutionalize "grabbing."
In a sharing model, lawyers gain the most by maximizing firm value, behavior which is more effective at creating firm capital.

Where a law- yer's income depends on the amount of work that he does for his clients, as it would under typical productivity formulas, the inde- pendence calculation shifts from the firm level to the level of the individual lawyer.

kp.k: Hours monitoring cannot fully resolve shirking
kp.d: Low recorded hours can reflect either insufficient effort or precisely the specialty downturns and personal misfortunes that sharing insures against. The authors propose comparisons within similarly exposed specialties, contextual assessment of personal difficulties and minimum hours rather than competitive hour rankings. Even these measures cannot reliably distinguish merely spending time from highly motivated, effective work.
qs: Shirking involves more than simply putting in too few hours.
Some of the problem disappears by simply setting a minimum number of hours that members of the relevant subgroup must work.
There is an enormous difference between the performance of a lawyer who is simply putting in his time and that of a lawyer who is truly motivated to produce.

kp.k: Professional culture links selection, training and promotion
kp.d: The authors hypothesize that selection and socialization create an internalized work ethic that controls otherwise hard-to-observe shirking. They connect this mechanism to elite-school and law-review recruitment, lengthy apprenticeship, mentoring and promotion-or-departure policies. They predict relatively little lateral partner hiring by sharing firms because lateral recruits lack the same screening and training, while greater emphasis on productivity should encourage permanent associates. These are proposed research hypotheses, not established findings.
qs: Through some combination of selection and socialization firms can create a powerful internalized work ethic.
Thus, we would expect sharing firms to engage in very little lateral hiring.
Thus, we expect that increasing emphasis on productivity should lead to renewed interest in the idea of permanent asso- ciates.

kp.k: Sophisticated general counsel shift power toward buyers
kp.d: Drawing substantially on contemporary anecdotal evidence, the authors identify expanding and increasingly capable in-house departments as the principal market change. General counsel act as purchasing agents, deciding what to internalize and which outside lawyers to retain. They predict that moving routine work in-house, internalizing client-specific coordination, using multiple firms and selecting individual specialists will reduce incumbent firms' advantages. Their suggestion that general counsel are becoming stronger bilateral negotiators is expressly a hunch without supporting data or a determinate theoretical result.
qs: Buy- ers are becoming much more sophisticated.
General counsel are the executives who decide what legal services are purchased and from whom.
We predict that more and more corporations will continue to bring routine or repetitive legal work in-house.
The catchphrase now is: "Shop for a lawyer, not a law firm."

kp.k: Predictions favor diversified firms without guaranteeing stability
kp.d: Looking forward from 1985, the authors predict that some leading firms will retain successful lockstep systems, while others will change compensation or split as firm-specific capital erodes. Productivity formulas alone will not create stability. They expect most future giants to remain existing giants because preserving accumulated capital is easier than creating it. They also predict that many boutiques will broaden services or merge, and that most undiversified boutiques will not outlive their founders, with stable-demand specialties such as tax and labor possible exceptions.
qs: First, we predict that boutique law firms-those that specialize in a single area-will not represent the wave of the future.
Absent such diversification, we predict that most bouti- ques will not have long-term institutional lives beyond the retire- ment of their founding partners.
We do not believe that this trend toward productivity formu- las will increase the stability of larger firms.
we think it is easier to retain firm-specific capital than to create it.

kp.k: Leadership and hybrid compensation can extend sharing
kp.d: The authors suggest that entrepreneurial leaders can create institutional capital by accepting less income than their individual contributions might command, thereby establishing a sharing culture. They also reject a binary choice between pure lockstep and pure productivity: firms can mix allocation principles, share returns beyond a productivity threshold, or insure only selected risks. One proposed limited bargain funds retraining after a specialty's collapse. The appropriate arrangement depends on the trade-off between diversification and incentives.
qs: Leadership of a particular sort may well provide the answer to this puzzle.
Both in theory and in practice, it is entirely possible for the method of profit division to reflect elements of both models.
they can limit the sharing bargain to providing the equivalent of disas- ter insurance.
then only to the extent necessary to retrain a lawyer in a new specialty.

kp.k: The authors explicitly resist universal conclusions
kp.d: The article calls for empirical and historical testing of compensation systems, specialty combinations and mechanisms restraining opportunism, including comparisons with accounting, advertising and investment banking. It closes by noting that two firms regarded as exceptionally profitable used different allocation principles: Cravath sharing and Skadden marginal product. Its conditional theory therefore does not establish one universally superior compensation system.
qs: Empirical and historical research may well make it possible to assess, refine, or possibly even reject our hypotheses about shar- ing.

Of the two firms widely considered to be the nation's most profitable, one- Cravath, Swaine & Moore-uses a sharing model and the other- Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom-follows a marginal product approach.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Gilson and Mnookin make no claims about AI. Their 1985 article offers economic explanations and predictions about corporate law firms, profit sharing and increasingly sophisticated purchasers of legal services.
pts.d: Recorded in the source's own domain, the authors argue that sharing partnership income diversifies lawyers' human-capital risks, but introduces incentives to shirk, demand larger profit shares or leave. Firm-specific capital constrains demands and departures, while selection, socialization and firm culture can constrain shirking. They predict that increasingly sophisticated general counsel will erode some firm-specific capital by internalizing routine work, reducing dependence on outside firms' client-specific knowledge and choosing individual specialists rather than relying on firm reputation. They predict continued diversification or merger of boutiques, survival of lockstep among some highly successful firms, and pressure on other firms to change compensation or split up. Moving to productivity-based compensation alone is not predicted to improve stability. Established large firms are expected to retain advantages over newcomers. These are historical legal-market claims, not predictions of AI-driven change.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The argument rests primarily on portfolio and agency theory, supported by historical descriptive statistics, reported firm experiences and explicitly qualified conjectures—not AI data or causal tests.
pts.d: Gilson and Mnookin use hypothetical examples to explain diversification and incentives; these are illustrations rather than measured outcomes. Historical background includes 1982 compensation statistics by firm size, Stanford graduate placements during 1977–1982, and comparisons of large-firm size in 1963 and 1983. Legal-press accounts of departures, firm collapses and compensation disputes illustrate organizational instability. Reports about Cravath and other sharing firms illustrate the coexistence of lockstep, profitability and stability. Accounts of expanding corporate legal departments and prominent lawyers becoming general counsel support the buyer-sophistication argument. The authors explicitly describe much of that support as anecdotal, acknowledge the lack of systematic empirical research on profit allocation, and invite research capable of rejecting their hypotheses. Reported observations and quotations from consultants are supporting material, not independent findings established by the authors.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The forecasts concern the 1980s and 1990s, including the decade following publication in January 1985, and depend on buyer sophistication and firms' capacity to maintain firm-specific capital.
pts.d: The article's references to the next ten years concern approximately 1985–1995, not the present AI era. The advantages of sharing depend on constraining shirking, grabbing and leaving. Lockstep survival is predicted particularly for firms with substantial existing firm-specific capital and supportive cultures. Competitive pressure is expected to diminish, not eliminate, such capital. Boutique longevity is qualified by diversification and the stability of demand in a specialty; tax and labor are offered as possible exceptions to the predicted difficulty of surviving founding partners. The authors allow successful productivity-based firms and hybrid compensation arrangements, rather than asserting universal superiority of any single formula.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are corporate law firms and their partners, specialist boutiques, associates, and corporate purchasers led by general counsel.
pts.d: Partners gain risk diversification from sharing but may face compensation disputes and departure incentives as firm-specific capital weakens. Established full-service firms may retain advantages from accumulated reputation, client relationships and organizational culture, while newer firms face greater difficulty creating those assets. Boutiques face concentrated specialty-demand risks. Associates are implicated through firms' profits on their work, lengthy partnership tracks, screening and socialization, and possible growth in permanent-associate roles under productivity-oriented compensation. Corporate clients and general counsel gain greater capacity to internalize work, compare providers, negotiate prices and move assignments between firms. The article does not establish effects on AI vendors, AI-related displacement or access to justice.
